note: Teaching text, clarifying questions, inferred constraints and own examples. Inferred, not official. Examples are small generated inputs with outputs from the independent references in oracles.py.

constraints: total nodes in params and returnType <= 2e4
clarifyingQuestions: What exact text format do nodes and function types use (separators, spaces, brackets)?
Can arguments themselves contain generics?
What should happen when an argument does not fit its parameter: error, exception or a sentinel?
Can a generic in the return type be absent from the parameters?
hints: Each node is either a string (primitive or generic) or a list (tuple); recurse on lists.
Format children first and join them with ", " inside square brackets.
The function type is the parameters joined with ", " inside parentheses, then " -> ", then the formatted return type.
invariants: the formatted string of a tuple starts with "[" and ends with "]"
formatting never changes the input nodes
tradeoffs: A recursive formatter is shortest; an explicit stack only matters for deeper nesting than the inferred 20 levels
hack2hire:69166e5710632c00111ca0eb.variantLabel: Inferred level 1: format a function type over primitives, generics and tuples

clarifyingQuestions: What exact text format do nodes and function types use (separators, spaces, brackets)?

A generic records the formatted argument it meets; a second meeting must give the same string.
After all parameters match, format the return type, printing a bound generic as its stored binding.

constraints: dates are valid days of 2000 to 2099 (days 01 to 28)
clarifyingQuestions: What exactly does each query count: policies per post, posts per policy, or log entries?
Is the date filter a single day or an inclusive range?
Are duplicate log lines counted once?
What do unknown ids return?
hints: Because logs are sorted by date, the logs inside a date range form one contiguous slice.
Group logs by post id and by policy so each group is itself sorted by date.
Binary-search the first date >= startDate and the first date > endDate in the right group, then count distinct keys in that slice with a set.
invariants: each group keeps the date order of the input
every count is a number of distinct keys, never of log lines
tradeoffs: Slices are counted per query (O(k)); offline distinct-count structures answer faster but are far more complex
hack2hire:68094bed31dc778b35c5d171.variantLabel: Inferred single variant: date-ranged unique violation counts

clarifyingQuestions: Are uppercase letters possible?
Does a substring have to contain only vowels, or only all five vowels?
Is the answer counted by position or by distinct text?
hints: A valid substring lies inside one maximal run of vowels.
For a fixed end, valid starts are the run start up to the smallest last position among the five vowels.
Track the last position of each vowel inside the current run and reset at every consonant.
invariants: last positions are only taken from the current run
the running total only grows
chooseWhen: Counting substrings with an at-least-once condition
tradeoffs: The per-end formula avoids a second pointer; a two-pointer window with counts generalises to other minimum-count conditions
hack2hire:67fdb0ced2adf72ba62b0eda.variantLabel: Inferred single variant: count all-vowel substrings containing every vowel

constraints: a closure names an open center and never the last open one
clarifyingQuestions: Is the capacity a per-visit burst or a lifetime limit?
What happens to packages when every center is full?
What is returned: per-center totals, the busiest center, or the assignments?
How are ties broken?
hints: Keep the current center and how many packages it has taken in this visit.
Keep the open centers in a circular linked list so the next open center is one pointer away.
On closing, unlink the center; if it was current, move the turn to its successor and reset the visit count.
invariants: the current center is always open
the visit count stays below the current center capacity
tradeoffs: A linked list makes removal O(1); a sorted set of open indices also works but costs a logarithm per step
hack2hire:699926ca6e73e4abccc9a376.variantLabel: Inferred single variant: round-robin bursts with closures, report the busiest center

clarifyingQuestions: Which item goes when several share the largest weight?
Can the item just inserted be evicted?
What does get return for a missing key?
Does get refresh anything?
hints: Track the total weight and a map from key to its current value, weight and write stamp.
A max-heap ordered by weight then by oldest stamp gives the eviction victim.
An update pushes a fresh heap entry; entries whose stamp no longer matches the map are stale and are skipped when popped.
invariants: the total weight equals the sum of the weights in the map
after every put the total is at most maxTotalWeight
chooseWhen: Caches with a size budget where big items are cheapest to drop
tradeoffs: Lazy deletion keeps updates O(log n) at the price of stale heap entries
hack2hire:68d30311d490dee995152f5b.variantLabel: Inferred single variant: weight-bounded cache evicting heaviest first

clarifyingQuestions: Must the pattern match the entire rest of the string or any substring?
Does "*" match the empty string?
What if the pattern starts with "*"?
Are other wildcards such as "?" possible?
hints: Split the pattern into star-free pieces.
If the first piece occurs at several places, the earliest occurrence leaves the most room for the remaining pieces.
Find each later piece greedily at its earliest position after the previous one, using a linear-time string search.
invariants: each piece is searched from where the previous match ended
the returned index is the start of the first piece occurrence
tradeoffs: Greedy piece matching is linear with KMP; built-in substring search can be quadratic on adversarial inputs
hack2hire:68815970f96758aa78e1d6b1.variantLabel: Inferred single variant: first start index of a wildcard substring match

constraints: every move joins adjacent dots inside the 9 x 9 grid
endpoints may be given in either order
clarifyingQuestions: Does completing a square give an extra turn?
What is returned on a tie?
Can endpoints be listed in either order?
Are invalid or repeated moves possible?
hints: Normalise each stick so its endpoints are in a fixed order, then store it in a set.
A horizontal stick borders the squares above and below it; a vertical one those left and right.
A bordering square is completed now if its other three sides are already placed; credit the player whose turn it is.
invariants: each square is credited at most once
player 1 moves at even 0-based indices
chooseWhen: Incremental scoring of local board events
tradeoffs: Checking only neighbouring squares is O(1) per move; full recounts are simpler but O(board) per move
hack2hire:69c81f4621f6ab4226966b28.variantLabel: Inferred single variant: dots-and-boxes winner with strict alternation

constraints: cells and word use letters A-Z and a-z
clarifyingQuestions: Must the word follow one direction, or may it turn?
Can a cell be reused?
Is the match case-sensitive?
hints: A straight-line word is fixed by its start cell and one of eight direction vectors.
Skip starts whose letter differs from word[0], and directions where the word would leave the board.
Compare letters step by step and stop at the first mismatch.
invariants: a straight line never revisits a cell
true is returned only after all letters matched
tradeoffs: Direct stepping needs no extra memory; precomputing all lines as strings uses O(mn) memory but enables substring search
hack2hire:68e86c2f80f69c7a01706886.variantLabel: Inferred single variant: word along one straight line in eight directions

clarifyingQuestions: What is returned: per-worker task lists, a map, or the final workloads?
How are specialties matched to tasks?
What happens to a task no worker can take?
Is there a limit on how many tasks a worker takes?
hints: Order workers by (workload, name).
A min-heap returns that minimum in O(log w); after assigning, reinsert the worker with its new workload.
Collect task ids per worker index and return them in input order.
invariants: each worker appears exactly once in the heap
workloads only grow
chooseWhen: Online load balancing with deterministic ties
tradeoffs: A heap is O(log w) per task; a linear scan is fine for few workers
hack2hire:697a5a552ae9e181e44b7b96.variantLabel: Inferred level 1: least-loaded assignment with name tie-break

clarifyingQuestions: What is returned: per-worker task lists, a map, or the final workloads?
How are specialties matched to tasks?
What happens to a task no worker can take?
Is there a limit on how many tasks a worker takes?
hints: Group workers by the types they handle.
Keep a min-heap per type; when a worker's workload changes, push a new entry into each of its type heaps.
When popping, discard entries whose recorded version is not the worker's current version.
invariants: a valid heap entry carries the worker's current workload
an unassigned task has no worker with its type
chooseWhen: Load balancing with skills or queues per category
tradeoffs: Lazy heaps duplicate entries across types; a balanced tree per type supports in-place updates instead
hack2hire:697a5dbe2ae9e181e44b7b9d.variantLabel: Inferred level 2: least-loaded assignment among specialists

clarifyingQuestions: What is returned: per-worker task lists, a map, or the final workloads?
How are specialties matched to tasks?
What happens to a task no worker can take?
Is there a limit on how many tasks a worker takes?
hints: Start from the level 2 lazy heaps per type.
A worker with a limit of 0 never enters the heaps.
After an assignment that reaches the limit, bump the version without pushing new entries.
invariants: no worker exceeds its limit
heap entries of a full worker are all stale
tradeoffs: Stale-entry skipping keeps removal cheap at the cost of extra heap entries

clarifyingQuestions: What is returned: the final array, or something per operation?
Is idx 0-indexed?
What does "2 idx" do on an index that is already 0?
hints: The leftmost 0 is the smallest index holding 0.
Keep candidate zero indices in a min-heap; push idx whenever "2 idx" writes a 0.
For "1", pop indices that are already 1 (stale) until the top holds a 0, then set it.
invariants: every index holding 0 is in the heap
the input array is never modified
tradeoffs: A heap with stale entries is simple; a segment tree or union-find over ones gives the same answers
hack2hire:69a35cd56e73e4abccc9bfb7.variantLabel: Inferred single variant: leftmost-zero fill and point resets, return final array

clarifyingQuestions: What is the third input?
What text format does the body use?
How are categories ordered?
What happens to detected words without a category?
hints: Map each keyword to its category first.
Walk the detected words once, counting each keyword inside its category in first-seen order.
Sort the category names and print one line per category.

counts sum to the number of mapped detections

clarifyingQuestions: May the balance reach exactly zero?
After the first failure, can the bank skip and continue?
Is the answer the count or the final balance?
hints: With prefix sums P, starting at s the balance after serving through k is initialBalance + P[k + 1] - P[s].
Serving from s stops at the first j > s with P[j] < P[s] - initialBalance.
Scanning starts from right to left, a stack of strictly smaller prefix values answers each "first smaller than" query by binary search.
invariants: the stack holds prefix values that decrease with distance
all sums stay below 2**53
chooseWhen: Longest feasible run from a free start under a running-balance constraint
tradeoffs: The stack answers threshold queries in O(log n); a sparse table of minima is an alternative with O(n log n) memory
hack2hire:6763722dcc8f5deed53ccd73.variantLabel: Inferred single variant: longest serviceable run after skipping a prefix

clarifyingQuestions: Can unary minus follow a binary operator, as in 2*-3?
Are spaces allowed?
How should division by zero or overflow be handled?
hints: Evaluate with two levels: a running sum of terms and the current term being multiplied or divided.
A parenthesis pushes the current state on a stack and starts fresh; ")" turns the finished sum into one operand.
Truncate toward zero exactly: divide magnitudes with integer division and restore the sign.
invariants: each frame is a sum of finished terms plus one open term
only "(" grows the stack, so recursion depth is never needed
tradeoffs: An explicit stack handles deep nesting; recursive descent is clearer but limited by the call stack
hack2hire:692d0f861abcca80b112238f.variantLabel: Inferred single variant: calculator with unary minus and truncating division

clarifyingQuestions: Are scores integers, floats or log-probabilities?
Is a sequence scored by the sum of its token scores?
In what order are the beam results returned and how are ties broken?
Do step scores depend on earlier tokens?
hints: Each step is independent.
Scan the step's scores keeping the best index.
Replace the best only on a strictly larger score so ties keep the smaller index.
invariants: the chosen index has the maximum score of its step
no smaller index has the same score
tradeoffs: Greedy decoding is optimal for a sum of independent step scores but not for conditional models

clarifyingQuestions: Are scores integers, floats or log-probabilities?
Is a sequence scored by the sum of its token scores?
In what order are the beam results returned and how are ties broken?
Do step scores depend on earlier tokens?
hints: Only the best beamWidth tokens of a step can appear in the next beam.
Compare candidates by total score; on equal totals the parent with the smaller lexicographic rank wins, then the smaller token.
Re-rank the surviving candidates lexicographically by (parent rank, token) for the next step.
invariants: the beam is sorted best first
lexicographic ranks are consistent with the actual index sequences
chooseWhen: Decoding with a bounded number of hypotheses
tradeoffs: Pruning tokens to the best beamWidth per step bounds work by k^2 per step instead of k V
hack2hire:6a4d62db60d5cca82da2fdda.variantLabel: Inferred level 2: beam search returning the final beam

constraints: coordinates are distinct and inside the grid
clarifyingQuestions: Is the output a count per k or the list of blocks?
Are blocks with zero black cells listed?
In which order are blocks listed?
hints: A black cell (x, y) lies in at most four blocks: corners (x - 1..x, y - 1..y) inside the grid.
Count each corner in a hash map keyed by the corner.
Bucket corners by count and sort each bucket.

each block appears in exactly one list
tradeoffs: A hash map is proportional to black cells; a dense array would need m n memory

clarifyingQuestions: May a block contain repeated letters?
Must every block be used?
Is the alphabet only lowercase letters?
hints: Positions and blocks form a bipartite graph: a position links to every block containing its letter.
The target is formable exactly when every position can be matched to a distinct block.
Augmenting paths (Kuhn) find a maximum matching; stop early if the target is longer than the number of blocks.
invariants: a matched block serves exactly one position
the matching size only grows
tradeoffs: Matching is polynomial where backtracking may be exponential; Hopcroft-Karp is faster for large graphs
